lead: The day after the feast of the Immaculate Conception, the readings take up its two great themes. Paul's hymn says that God chose us in Christ “before the foundation of the world”, to be holy and blameless. Luke shows the moment when one young woman of Nazareth, already prepared by God, says yes. God's plan is older than the world, and it passes through one person's willing word of consent.

r.h: Chosen before the foundation of the world
set: The letter comes from prison (3:1; 4:1) and is traditionally by Paul. Some of the oldest manuscripts lack the words “in Ephesus” in 1:1, and many scholars think it was meant for several churches of the region; some think a later disciple wrote it. In Greek, vv. 3–14 are one long sentence of blessing, shaped like the Jewish berakah, the prayer that begins “Blessed be God”. Today's reading takes most of it.
str: v. 3: the blessing: God has blessed us in Christ.
vv. 4–6: chosen and adopted, to the praise of his grace.
vv. 7–8: redemption and forgiveness through his blood.
vv. 9–10: the mystery made known: all things gathered up in Christ.
vv. 11–12: our inheritance and our hope.
kw: The same root is used three times in v. 3. We bless God because he first blessed us.
In Paul not a riddle, but God's hidden plan, now made known (v. 9).
To bring together under one head. St Irenaeus built on this idea: Christ sums up in himself the whole of creation and human history, and heals it (in substance; CCC 518).
vv: just as he chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless before him in love.
Choice comes first, holiness follows. We are not chosen because we are holy, but so that we may become holy. The word “blameless” is also used of an unblemished sacrifice.
He destined us for adoption as his children through Jesus Christ,
Adoption was a serious legal act in the Roman world: the adopted son received the full rights of a son. By baptism, God's only Son shares his place with us.
as a plan for the fullness of time, to gather up all things in him, things in heaven and things on earth.
Salvation is not only for souls. The whole universe is to find its head and its peace in Christ.
ch: The Catechism applies these words directly to Mary: the Father blessed her more than any other created person with every spiritual blessing and chose her in Christ before the foundation of the world, to be holy and blameless (CCC 492). It also takes this hymn as the model of all Christian liturgy, which blesses the Father for his blessings (CCC 1077–1083). What God did perfectly in Mary is what he wants for each of us.

r.h: Here am I, the servant of the Lord
set: Gabriel has greeted a young woman of Nazareth, engaged to Joseph of the house of David, and has told her that she will bear a son, the heir of David's throne (1:26–33). In the Jewish custom of the time, engagement was a binding legal bond, though the couple did not yet live together. Nazareth was a small, unimportant village of Galilee. Our reading is the second half of the scene: her question and her answer.
str: v. 35: the angel's answer: the Holy Spirit, the power of the Most High, the Son of God.
vv. 36–37: a sign, Elizabeth, and the reason: nothing is impossible with God.
v. 38: Mary's consent; the angel leaves.
kw: The same verb is used in the Greek of Exodus 40:35 for the cloud of God's glory covering the tent, and in Luke 9:34 for the cloud at the Transfiguration. Mary becomes the new place of God's presence.
A woman slave. Mary takes this as a title of honour, in the line of Moses and David, who were called servants of the Lord.
A form of the Greek verb that expresses a wish. Mary does not merely accept; she desires what God desires.
vv: Mary said to the angel, “How can this be, since I am a virgin?”
The Greek says, “since I do not know a man”, which the POC keeps. “Know” is the biblical word for marital union. Her question is about how, not whether.
For nothing will be impossible with God.”
These words echo what the Lord said to Abraham about Sarah (Genesis 18:14 in Greek). The God of the first barren mother is the God of Elizabeth and of the virgin of Nazareth.
Then Mary said, “Here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word.”
After this Luke simply says that the angel departed. She is left with the promise, and no further explanation.
ch: The Catechism presents Mary's answer as the obedience of faith (CCC 148, 494). St Irenaeus, quoted there, says that the knot of Eve's disobedience was loosed by Mary's obedience, and Lumen Gentium 56 teaches that she was not a passive instrument but cooperated by her faith and obedience. St Augustine says that she conceived Christ in her heart by faith before she conceived him in her womb (in substance). St Bernard of Clairvaux, in a famous homily, imagines the whole world waiting for her reply (in substance).

qa: Zechariah was struck silent for asking a question. Why was Mary not?

The two questions differ. Zechariah asks for a guarantee: “How will I know that this is so?” (1:18), and the angel himself says that he did not believe (1:20). Mary already accepts the promise and asks how it will come about, since she does not know a man. Elizabeth later says of her, “blessed is she who believed” (1:45).
study: Ephesians says that I was chosen before the world began. How would it change my day if I really believed this?
Mary's “let it be” was said with no further explanation given to her. What is God asking of me that I do not yet fully understand?
